Thomas Shepard
TOM-uhs SHEP-erd
proper noun
Aramaic given name Thomas, “a twin”; the surname Shepard, a variant of shepherd, “one who tends sheep.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Thomas Shepard (1605–1649) was an English-born Puritan who, driven from his homeland by Laudian persecution, crossed to New England and became the founding pastor of the church at Cambridge in Massachusetts, hard by the new college that would be named Harvard. Educated at Cambridge in England, Shepard was a preacher of singular searching power and a leading figure in the spiritual life of the early colony. He is remembered for his treatises The Sincere Convert and The Sound Believer, and above all for The Parable of the Ten Virgins Opened and Applied, a great body of sermons upon Matthew twenty-five that anatomizes the difference between the wise and foolish, the true believer and the false professor. Shepard preached preparation, conviction, and the absolute necessity of regenerating grace, refusing all false comfort and pressing his hearers to examine whether their oil was the genuine work of the Spirit or a mere outward profession that would fail at the bridegroom’s coming. He took a leading part against the antinomian errors that troubled the colony, contending for sound doctrine joined to holy life. His Autobiography and Journal reveal a heart of deep humility and self-jealousy before God. Shepard stands among the choicest of the New England divines, a faithful shepherd who fed the flock and warned the careless, exalting sovereign grace and the necessity of the new birth.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A New England Puritan, founding pastor at Cambridge, author of The Sincere Convert and The Parable of the Ten Virgins.

expand to see more

THOMAS SHEPARD, English-born Puritan (1605–1649), founding pastor of the church at Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Driven to New England by Laudian persecution, educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge.

Author of The Sincere Convert, The Sound Believer, and The Parable of the Ten Virgins.

A leading opponent of the antinomian errors that troubled the early colony.

He pressed conviction, preparation, and the necessity of regenerating grace (Mat 25:13).

📖 Key Scripture

Mat 25:13 — "Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh."

Mat 25:4 — "But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps."

2Co 13:5 — "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?"

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Shepard’s searching call to true conversion is recovered against an age of easy assurance that never tests whether the lamp holds oil.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Shepard’s ministry rebukes the modern aversion to self-examination and the cheap assurance that pronounces every professor saved. Shepard opened the parable of the ten virgins to show that the foolish, too, had lamps and a profession, yet wanted the oil of true grace and were shut out at the last. He refused false comfort and pressed his hearers to prove whether Christ was truly in them, knowing that a hope untried is a hope undone.

The lesson to recover is the necessity of the new birth and of watchfulness against the bridegroom’s coming. Shepard teaches that men may resemble the saved in much and yet be strangers to regenerating grace; therefore the soul must examine itself and seek the genuine oil of the Spirit. To watch, to be ready, to be truly converted—this is no harsh demand but the mercy of a faithful shepherd warning the careless of the door that shuts.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Thomas means “a twin”; Shepard is a variant of shepherd, “one who tends the flock.”

expand to see more

Thomas — from Aramaic T’oma, “a twin.”

Shepard, a variant of shepherd, from Old English scēaphierde, “sheep-herder.”

Convert, from the Latin convertere, “to turn about,” one turned from sin to God.

Virgin, from the Latin virgo, here the ten of the parable awaiting the bridegroom (Mat 25:13).

Watch, rendering the Greek grēgoreite, “be vigilant, stay awake” (Mat 25:13).

Usage

"Thomas Shepard opened the parable of the ten virgins to test every false profession."

"Driven from England, Thomas Shepard founded the church at Cambridge in New England."

"Thomas Shepard preached the new birth with a searching power few could equal."
